strengths: The paper is well-motivated and clearly connects on-policy actor optimization to a classification-style (cross-entropy) view versus a regression-style (squared-error) view, providing a coherent conceptual framing for why discretized categorical actors combined with architectural improvements from supervised learning should help.

Proposition 4.1 gives a clean, interpretable theoretical result comparing REINFORCE gradient variance for Gaussian vs. categorical policies in a simplified one-step setting, with a proof in the appendix, offering some formal grounding for the empirical claims.

The empirical evaluation is broad: three on-policy algorithms (PPO, TRPO, SPO), three benchmark families (Gym locomotion, ManiSkill state-based, ManiSkill RGB-based), and multiple seeds with confidence intervals, showing consistent improvements of RN-D over Gaussian and standard-MLP baselines across most settings.

The loss-swap ablation (Appendix C.2) is a valuable design that disentangles the effect of discretized action representation from the effect of the cross-entropy-like objective, strengthening the causal claim that the classification-style loss (not just discretization) drives the improvement.

Additional ablations on actor-network scaling, bin-count sensitivity, gradient-variance/SNR analysis, and runtime overhead provide a reasonably thorough characterization of the method's behavior and practical cost.
Comparisons to representative off-policy baselines (TD3, TD-MPC2) and wall-clock analysis help contextualize the practical value of the approach beyond only on-policy competitors.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is a combination of two largely known ingredients (categorical/discretized actors from Tang & Agrawal 2020 and Zhu et al. 2024; residual+LayerNorm MLP backbones from SimBa/BroNet), and the paper explicitly acknowledges it introduces no new architectural module, which limits originality.

The paper deliberately avoids comparison against the more sophisticated discretization schemes it cites as directly related work (ordinal parameterizations of Tang & Agrawal; unimodal/Poisson-based parameterizations of Zhu et al.), which could be stronger baselines/ablations than plain uniform softmax discretization; without these comparisons it is unclear whether RN-D's gains stem mainly from the regularized network or would be further amplified/diminished when combined with these more structured discretized actors.

Proposition 4.1 relies on a highly simplified one-step, constant-return REINFORCE setting that does not directly model the multi-epoch, clipped, advantage-weighted PPO updates used in the actual experiments, so its practical relevance to explaining the observed training dynamics is more suggestive than rigorously established.

Main results are reported primarily via aggregate learning-curve plots rather than numerical tables with exact final scores and confidence intervals, making precise quantitative comparison, effect-size assessment, and reproducibility checks harder for readers.

Hyperparameters (including entropy coefficient set to 0, and other defaults) are held fixed from existing codebases across all four actor variants without task-specific tuning; this raises the possibility that baselines (especially MLP-C, the dominant standard implementation) are undertuned relative to what practitioners typically use, potentially inflating the perceived gap.

The bin-count ablation shows that performance degrades noticeably as K grows large and the ideal range is fairly narrow and task-dependent, suggesting the method requires non-trivial tuning of discretization granularity, somewhat undercutting the “simple drop-in replacement” framing.

The actor-critic interaction is left unexplored (critic architecture is held fixed throughout), which is a reasonable scoping choice but limits the paper's ability to draw conclusions about jointly scaling networks in on-policy RL, an important aspect given the framing around network capacity and classification-style optimization.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: revisits actor parameterization/architecture as an underexplored lever in on-policy RL, connecting classification-style objectives (used successfully for value learning) to policy learning.

Rigorous theoretical contribution: Proposition 4.1 provides a clean, fully proven comparison of REINFORCE gradient variance between Gaussian and categorical policies, giving a principled (if stylized) explanation for why categorical actors may exhibit lower gradient variance, especially as Gaussian std shrinks during training.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 5 Gym locomotion tasks, 10 ManiSkill state-based tasks, and 5 ManiSkill RGB tasks, with consistent 2x2 factorial ablation (discrete vs continuous x regularized vs MLP network) isolating the individual and combined effects of policy parameterization and architecture.

The loss-swap ablation (Appendix C.2) is a well-designed control experiment that convincingly disentangles the benefit of the discretized action representation from the cross-entropy-style optimization objective, showing the latter is the dominant factor.

Additional scaling studies (actor width, number of bins) and comparisons against strong off-policy/model-based baselines (TD3, TD-MPC2) add useful practical insight and situate the method relative to the broader continuous-control literature.
Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameter tables, environment descriptions, and normalization procedures are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is limited: the categorical actor idea builds directly on Tang & Agrawal (2020)/Zhu et al. (2024), and the regularized residual+LayerNorm architecture is explicitly adapted from SimBa/BroNet-style designs (the paper itself states the contribution is not a new network module). The paper is primarily a careful empirical combination/ablation study rather than a fundamentally new method.

No empirical comparison against the more sophisticated ordinal or unimodal (Poisson-based) discretized actor parameterizations from the closely related prior work (Tang & Agrawal 2020; Zhu et al. 2024), despite these being the most directly comparable baselines for the discretization component; the paper only compares to a 'simplest baseline' softmax discretization, leaving open whether RN-D's advantage would persist against stronger discretization schemes.

Performance is shown to be quite sensitive to the number of bins K (Appendix C.4), yet no principled method for choosing K is proposed; this introduces an additional hyperparameter whose optimal value seems task/architecture dependent, undermining the 'simple drop-in change' framing.

The SOTA/wall-clock comparisons against TD3 and TD-MPC2 (Appendix C.1) are conducted only on 2 of the 20 evaluated tasks and across non-identical hardware (H800/RTX5090 vs A200), and TD-MPC2 is evaluated with only 3 seeds versus 5 for the proposed method, weakening the strength of the 'state-of-the-art' claim in the abstract.

Proposition 4.1 relies on a simplified one-step REINFORCE toy setting with constant returns and a fixed covariance; the extrapolation of this insight to the full PPO clipped-surrogate setting with learned, state-dependent variance is asserted qualitatively but not formally justified or empirically verified beyond a single aggregate variance plot (Fig. 4).

The paper lacks an explicit Limitations section; issues surfaced in the paper's own ablations (bin-count sensitivity, non-monotonic returns with actor width, entropy coefficient fixed to 0) are not synthesized into a discussion of when the method might fail or require tuning.
The Impact Statement is boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with any ethical or societal considerations specific to the work.
